questions.question: Geologists use two words for the ways water, wind and ice wear the land down: weathering and erosion. What is the difference between the two?
questions.answer: Weathering breaks rock up, and erosion carries it away
choices: Weathering breaks rock up, and erosion carries it away
Erosion breaks rock up, and weathering carries it away
Weathering happens slowly, and erosion happens fast
Weathering happens on land, and erosion happens in water
questions.context: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it lies, the work of ice in cracks, growing roots and blown sand. Erosion carries the pieces off by running water, wind, ice or gravity, and deposition drops them somewhere new. Either one can be slow or fast, on land or under the sea.
questions.grade_note: Telling weathering (breaking in place) from erosion (carrying away) is the core of TEKS 5.10C and NGSS 4-ESS2-1, and mixing up the two words is a well-studied student error.

questions.question: Rain trickles into a crack in a boulder high on a mountain. On cold nights the water in the crack freezes, and after many winters of freezing and thawing, the boulder splits apart. Why does freezing water split rock?
questions.answer: Water takes up more space as ice
choices: Water takes up more space as ice
Water takes up less space as ice
Ice weighs more than the water did
Ice is harder than the rock is
questions.context: Water swells by nearly a tenth as it freezes, so ice in a crack pushes the rock apart, and each thaw lets water creep a little deeper. Ice weighs just the same as the water it came from and is far softer than rock; it splits the boulder by needing more room.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 4-ESS2-1 names cycles of freezing and thawing as a cause of weathering, and water freezing in cracks is the standard 5th-grade example of it.

questions.question: A seed lands in a narrow crack in a boulder and sprouts into a young tree, sending its roots down into the crack. What will the roots do to the boulder over many years?
questions.answer: Push the crack wider until the rock splits
choices: Push the crack wider until the rock splits
Hold the two sides of the crack together
Fill the crack so no water can freeze in it
Do nothing, since rock is too hard for roots
questions.context: Roots thicken as they grow, and in a crack they pry the rock apart like a slowly driven wedge, which is a kind of weathering. In loose soil roots do the opposite and hold it in place, but in solid rock they break it.
questions.grade_note: Plant roots breaking rock is one of the weathering agents 5th graders learn (NGSS 4-ESS2-1 lists vegetation), alongside ice and wind.

questions.question: A deep, narrow canyon winds for many kilometres across a high plateau. Its steep rock walls drop hundreds of metres to the canyon floor. What made the canyon?
questions.answer: A river slowly cutting down through the rock
choices: A river slowly cutting down through the rock
An earthquake suddenly splitting the ground open
The wind slowly blowing the rock away
A volcano suddenly blasting the rock apart
questions.context: Rivers carve canyons. The sand and stones in the water scrape the riverbed like sandpaper and cut it a little deeper each year, so a deep canyon can take millions of years. Earthquakes crack the ground, but they do not open canyons.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.10C names canyons as landforms 5th graders must explain, and the standard teaching is that a river cuts one over a very long time.

questions.question: A delta is a wide, flat stretch of land at the mouth of a river, where it flows into the sea. How does a delta form?
questions.answer: The river drops the mud and sand it carries
choices: The river drops the mud and sand it carries
The river cuts the coast into a new shape
The wind heaps sand up along the shore
The ground there is pushed up from below
questions.context: A river slows down as it runs into the still sea, and slow water cannot carry as much, so it drops its mud and sand. This dropping is called deposition, and over many years it builds new land out into the sea. The name comes from the Greek letter delta, a triangle, the shape many deltas take.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.10C names deltas, and 5th graders learn that a delta is built where a river drops its sediment at its mouth.

questions.question: Water, wind and ice each build or carve their own kinds of landforms. Which of these landforms does the wind make?
choices: Sand dunes
Deltas
Canyons
U-shaped valleys
questions.context: Wind bounces sand grains along close to the ground and drops them where it slows, heaping them into dunes in deserts and along beaches; the dunes creep downwind year by year. Rivers build deltas and cut canyons, and glaciers carve U-shaped valleys.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.10C names sand dunes beside deltas and canyons, and matching each landform to the wind, water or ice that made it is the standard 5th-grade task.

questions.question: High in the mountains, a valley has steep walls and a wide, rounded floor, so that it is shaped like the letter U. What carved this valley?
choices: A glacier
A river
The wind
An earthquake
questions.context: A glacier is a huge mass of ice that creeps slowly downhill, grinding the rock with stones frozen into its base and tearing out blocks as it goes. It scrapes the sides as well as the floor and leaves a U shape. A river cuts mostly downward and leaves a narrower valley shaped like a V.
questions.grade_note: The curriculum line for this grade (G5.E5) names glacier-carved valleys, and the U shape is the mark by which a glacier's valley is told from a river's V.

questions.question: On most days a mountain stream moves only sand and small pebbles. After a heavy storm it swells into a flood that sweeps boulders downstream. Why can the flood move the boulders?
questions.answer: The water is moving much faster
choices: The water is moving much faster
The boulders float in the deeper water
The storm's wind pushes the boulders
The rain makes the riverbed slippery
questions.context: The faster water flows, the bigger the rocks it can push and carry, so a flood moves boulders that sit still on a calm day. Rock is more than twice as dense as water, so a boulder never floats, however deep the stream.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 4-ESS2-1 has students test how the slope and volume of flowing water change erosion, and floods are among the fast changes 5th-grade units teach.

questions.question: Most changes to the land are slow, taking thousands of years or more, but a few are fast. Which of these can change the land in a few minutes?
questions.answer: A landslide pouring down a hillside
choices: A landslide pouring down a hillside
A glacier carving out a valley
Tree roots prying a boulder apart
The wind piling sand into a dune
questions.context: In a landslide, gravity pulls a mass of rock and soil down a slope, often after heavy rain soaks the ground or an earthquake shakes it, and the fastest are over in seconds or minutes. Glaciers, roots and wind do their work over many years.
questions.grade_note: Students learn from 2nd grade (NGSS 2-ESS1-1) that Earth events can be quick or slow, and 5th-grade units on shaping the land add landslides and floods as the fast ones.
